ch1-open.title: Signing in
ch1-open.standfirst: Every visit to Canvas M starts at the same door. This chapter walks through the three ways in — an email and password, a one-time link by email, or a meeting invite — plus the language and theme controls that live on the card, and the exact words the screen shows when something goes wrong.

ch1-paths.heading: Sign in to Canvas M
steps: Open your Canvas M link. Staff land on the sign-in card; guests on a one-time invite.
Staff: enter your work email and password.
Guests: open the invite link — no password needed.
Set your language and theme from the top-right switcher anytime.

note.html: The whole app — and this book — comes in English, 한국어, and Tiếng Việt.

ch2-open.title: Joining a meeting
ch2-open.standfirst: Every meeting in Canvas M is reached the same way: you sign in, you pick the meeting from your list, and the app routes you to whichever door is open for you. This chapter walks the whole path — from the meeting list, through the waiting screens, to the moment your microphone goes live.

ch2-concept.eyebrow: Before you start · The mental model
ch2-concept.heading: What the waiting room is for
ch2-concept.lead: Some rooms open straight away; others ask you to knock. The waiting room is simply a held space — the host sees your name and lets you in when the meeting is ready. Nothing you do there is visible to the room, and you always arrive muted.
ch2-concept.body: Think of it as the corridor outside a studio: you hear nothing through the door, and nobody inside hears you. The moment the host admits you, your microphone is still off — you choose when to speak.
ch2-concept.pull: You never enter a meeting already talking. The first word is always yours to give.

diagram.label: FIG. 2.0 — FLOW
diagram.cap: knock → host admits → you join (muted) → unmute when ready

note.html: If no one answers within ~30 seconds, you can knock again — your place is not lost.

ch2-join.heading: Join with a link or code
steps: Open the invite link, or click Join on your dashboard.
If asked, type the 6-digit code from your invite.
Choose whether to turn on your camera — your microphone stays off until you unmute.
Press Join meeting.

note.html: Closing the tab cancels your knock — keep it open while you wait.

host.html: Admitting people and locking the room are the host's controls — you won't see them as a participant.

legend.text: Your knock status & name
The host's admit prompt
Re-knock, after 30 seconds

ch3-open.title: Be seen & heard
ch3-open.standfirst: Joining a Canvas M meeting never forces your microphone on. You enter as a quiet listener, then choose — one button at a time — when to speak, when to show your camera, when to raise your hand, and when to react. This chapter walks every one of those controls, exactly as they appear in the meeting header, and every state they can show.

ch3-mic.heading: Speak when you're ready
steps: In the live cluster, find the microphone icon. Right after you join it shows “Unmute” on hover — you are connected but silent.
Click it once. The browser asks for microphone permission now (this first click is what acquires the mic), then your audio goes live and the tooltip flips to “Mute”.
Click again to mute. The icon switches to a struck-through mic, turns red, and the tooltip reads “Unmute”.
Watch your own avatar tile in the people strip: a green dot means your mic is live; a red mic-off badge means you're muted.
ch3-mic.outcome: Your mic toggles between live and muted with a single click. The permission prompt only ever fires on the very first unmute — a deliberate user gesture — never on join.
ch3-mic.note: If your device has no microphone at all, the mic button is disabled and its tooltip reads “This device has no microphone — listen only”. You can still hear everyone; you simply can't transmit.

host.html: A host can mute you from the participants panel. If that happens your mic button shows muted and you'll need to unmute yourself again to speak.

ch4-open.title: Video layouts
ch4-open.standfirst: Canvas M lets you choose how everyone's camera tiles sit around your shared canvas. Pick a quiet strip, a docked rail, or a full-screen grid — and pin the one face you want to keep watching. This chapter walks every surface, every toggle, and the gentle rules behind who lands centre stage.

ch4-layouts.heading: Three ways to see the room

tiles.cap: A slim avatar strip. The canvas stays full-size — best for drawing.
A rail of camera tiles along the bottom; the canvas slides up to make room.
A full-screen grid of everyone. Tap a tile to pin them as the focus.

ch4-layouts.useWhen: Switch any time from Video layout in the header. Your choice is remembered on this device — and in Gallery you can flip between Grid and Speaker.

ch5-open.title: Presence & focus
ch5-open.standfirst: Who is in the room, who is speaking, and where everyone is looking. This chapter covers the participant strip, raising your hand, sending reactions, following another person's view, pinning a face, and the three video surfaces plus the floating presenter window — all the quiet signals that keep a meeting in sync without anyone saying a word.

ch5-present.heading: Keep a face in view while you work
ch5-present.lead: The floating presenter is a small camera window that hovers over the canvas, so the person speaking stays visible even in minimal layout. Drag it anywhere; Minimise tucks it away, Hide closes it, and Reopen presenter window brings it back.
ch5-present.body: Presence is the quiet layer of a meeting — who has a hand up, who is speaking, who is following whom. None of it interrupts the canvas; it simply tells the room where attention is.
ch5-present.pull: You're never just a name in a list — the room can always see you're there.

diagram.label: FIG. 5.1 — PRESENTER
diagram.cap: drag · minimise · hide · reopen

ch5-focus.heading: Raise a hand, react, or follow

tiles.cap: Press Raise hand — a marker shows on your tile until you Lower hand.
Open Reactions and send 👍 ❤️ 😂 🎉 👏 😮 — it floats up for everyone.
Click a participant to follow their view; your canvas tracks theirs until you Stop.

ch5-focus.useWhen: Following is great for a walkthrough — let the presenter steer while your screen mirrors exactly what they pan and zoom to.

ch6-open.title: Backgrounds & quality
ch6-open.standfirst: Two different backgrounds live in Canvas M, and they are easy to confuse. One dresses your dashboard desk with a wallpaper; the other replaces or blurs what sits behind you on camera during a meeting. This chapter walks through both, plus the video-quality ceiling that decides how sharp your camera looks to everyone else. Every setting here is a per-browser cosmetic choice: it lives on this device, survives a reload, and is never synced to your account.

ch6-set.heading: Blur or replace your background
steps: Turn your camera on, then open Change / blur background.
Pick Blur — choose Light, Medium, or Strong.
Or pick a scene under Backgrounds: Forest mist, Crystal leaves, or Office.
Choose No background to go back to your raw camera.
Open Video quality and set Auto, Low, Medium, or High.
ch6-set.outcome: Your background and quality apply instantly and stick on this device.

note.html: Background effects are desktop-only — on an iPad or phone the control is hidden. Auto quality adapts to your network up to any cap your admin sets.

ch6-blur.heading: Three strengths of blur

tiles.cap: A gentle softening — the room is still readable behind you.
A balanced blur for most desks. The usual choice.
Fully obscured — nothing behind you is legible.

ch6-blur.useWhen: Blur when the room is busy; pick an image scene when you'd rather not show the room at all.

ch7-open.title: Canvas basics
ch7-open.standfirst: The shared canvas is where the meeting actually happens. This chapter walks the toolbar tool by tool, shows the Canvas M extras tucked beside it, and explains how to place things, move the camera, and read the mini-map — all from a participant's seat.

ch7-draw.heading: Draw on the shared canvas
steps: Pick a tool from the toolbar: select, rectangle, ellipse, arrow, line, draw, or text.
Click or drag on the canvas to place it — everyone sees it appear live.
Press <kbd>V</kbd> for select, then drag to move or resize what you made.
Open Canvas navigation to Zoom in, Zoom out, or reset to 100%.
Drag on the minimap to move the camera across a big board.
ch7-draw.outcome: Your marks appear for the whole room the instant you draw them.

note.html: Everything is collaborative in real time — your cursor and edits stream to everyone, and theirs to you.

ch7-anatomy.heading: Everything on the canvas, labelled
ch7-anatomy.standfirst: The toolbar groups your tools left to right; the navigator sits bottom-right. Five places to know.

legend.text: Select / move (V)
Shapes — rectangle, ellipse, arrow, line
Freehand draw & text
MCM extras — stickers, stamps, viewers, bot
Navigation map — zoom & minimap

ch8-open.title: Decorate & annotate
ch8-open.standfirst: Stickers, stamps, revision clouds, and author badges turn a working canvas into a marked-up one. This chapter covers every decoration tool a participant can reach — where the buttons live, how placing mode behaves, and what each one leaves behind on the shared scene.

ch8-decor.heading: Mark up the board

tiles.cap: Open the picker, scroll to resize, then click to place. Pick Stickers or Stamps.
Draw a cloud around a change and drop a Note where you want attention.
Toggle Show authors to reveal who drew each element; Hide authors clears it.

ch8-decor.useWhen: Use a revision cloud to call out exactly what changed; turn on authors when you need to know whose mark is whose.

ch9-open.title: Translate & the Canvas Bot
ch9-open.standfirst: Two pieces of on-canvas intelligence live side by side: a Translate pill that turns any text you select into Vietnamese, English or Korean, and the MCM Bot you drop anywhere on the board to summarise, list decisions, or answer a question about the meeting. Both write real canvas elements, so everyone in the room sees the result.

ch9-translate.heading: Translate text right on the board
ch9-translate.lead: Select a text element and press Translate — the text is rendered in your language in place. If the original changes, the translation is marked out of date; press Refresh translation to update it.
ch9-translate.body: Pick a different target any time with Choose another language. The translation is yours — it doesn't change what anyone else sees on the canvas.

diagram.label: FIG. 9.0 — TRANSLATE
diagram.cap: select text → Translate → reads in your language

ch9-bot.heading: Ask the bot to draw an answer
ch9-bot.lead: Open Ask MCM Bot from the toolbar, click the canvas to drop the prompt, and type a request — "summarize the meeting", "list decisions", or a design question.
ch9-bot.body: The bot reads the meeting's chat, the live transcript, and the canvas text, then writes its answer onto the board at the point you chose. Nothing fires on its own — the bot only runs when you ask.
ch9-bot.pull: Before: a blank corner of the board. After: a written summary the whole room can read and keep.

diagram.label: FIG. 9.1 — BOT
diagram.cap: drop prompt → ask → answer drawn on canvas

note.html: Only the resulting text is shared with the room — your prompt box is local to you.

ch10-open.title: Screen sharing
ch10-open.standfirst: One presenter at a time, broadcast live to the whole room. Share your screen with a single click, or watch someone else's in a floating viewer you can pop onto a second monitor. This chapter covers presenting, watching, audio, and every state the button can be in.

ch10-share.heading: Present your screen
steps: Press Present in the header, then Share screen.
Choose a screen, window, or browser tab in your browser's prompt.
While you present, a banner reads You are presenting.
Press Stop sharing when you're done.
Watching someone else? Use Pop out to move their share to another monitor.
ch10-share.outcome: Your screen appears for everyone in the room.

note.html: Only one person shares at a time. If someone else is presenting you'll see {name} is presenting — wait for them to finish. Screen sharing isn't supported on iPad or iPhone — present from a computer.

ch10-watch.heading: When someone else presents
steps: Do nothing — the floating viewer appears automatically the moment a presenter starts. Its header reads "{name} is presenting" with a live indicator dot.
Use the — (minimize) button in the viewer header to collapse it to just the title bar when you need the canvas, then ▢ (Expand) to bring the picture back.
If your browser supports it, use the ⧉ button (Pop out) to float the share in a separate, draggable window — handy for a second monitor (see the next section).
Live captions, when on, pin to the bottom edge of the viewer so you can follow along with the spoken audio.

When the presenter stops or leaves, the viewer closes by itself. If they only minimised their shared window, the picture pauses and recovers automatically when it reappears — you don't need to do anything.
ch10-watch.outcome: You see the presenter's live screen in a movable viewer, with captions and any shared audio carried along with it.
ch10-watch.note: You join the share silently to watch — Canvas M never prompts for your camera or microphone just to receive someone's screen.
ch10-watch.figcap: The floating viewer: title "{name} is presenting", a Pop out button, and a Minimize / Expand toggle.

ch11-open.title: The meeting library
ch11-open.standfirst: Every image, drawing, document and 3D model the room shares lives in one shelf. This chapter shows you how to add a file, find it again, place it on the canvas, and keep it from being deleted out from under you.

ch11-place.heading: Put a file on the canvas
steps: Click a tile to drop it at the centre of your current view.
Or drag a tile onto the canvas to place it exactly where you let go.
Images land at their natural size (capped so large pictures stay sane); DXF, PDF and IFC land at a sensible default frame you can resize with the normal selection handles.
PDFs open on page 1 — advance pages later from the focus toolbar on the placed document.
Click the tile again and Canvas M jumps to the copy already on the canvas instead of dropping a duplicate.
ch11-place.outcome: The file appears as a normal canvas element that everyone in the room can see, move, and draw on top of.
ch11-place.note: Pen strokes, shapes and stickers you add after a PDF or IFC sit on top of it via the usual “Bring to Front” ordering, because those anchors are real image elements on the canvas — not a separate overlay.
ch11-place.figcap: Click to insert at centre; drag to place at the drop point.

ch11-types.heading: What the library accepts
rows: Place, pin, and annotate like any drawing.
Page through and mark up; see Chapter 12.
Orbit in 3D, isolate storeys, section the model.

note.html: Anything else is skipped with a notice. Chat attachments are images only.

ch12-open.title: Viewing documents
ch12-open.standfirst: A PDF spec, a DXF floor plan, an IFC building model — Canvas M opens all three right on the shared canvas. Turn pages, toggle layers, orbit a 3D model, slice it, measure it. Everyone in the room sees the page you land on; the rest of the controls are yours to explore at your own pace.

Fit · Storeys · Objects tree
Style — Shaded / Clay / Wireframe — and Ghost
Measure & Section the model

Fit to frame — reset the view

ch13-open.title: Chat
ch13-open.standfirst: The Conversation panel is the room's running text channel. Type a line, mention a file, summon the AI, react with a tap, quote a reply, and read every message in your own language — all from one quiet, two-row composer beside the canvas.

ch13-send.heading: Send a message
steps: Click the text area — its placeholder reads Type a message….
Type your line. The card highlights once there is non-blank text, and the Send button enables.
Press <kbd>Enter</kbd> to send. Use <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd> for a line break without sending.
Or click the Send (paper-plane) button on the right of the action row.
ch13-send.outcome: Your message appears at the bottom of the stream under your avatar and the label You, and the panel scrolls to it. Empty or whitespace-only drafts are ignored — Send stays disabled until you type something.
ch13-send.note: Messages are sent end-to-end encrypted with the room key. The stream auto-scrolls to the newest message whenever the count changes, so you always land on the latest line.

ch13-xlate.heading: Read every message in your language
ch13-xlate.lead: Turn on Auto-translate at the top of the chat and incoming messages arrive in your language automatically — the original stays one tap away.
ch13-xlate.body: It's a per-person setting: you read in your language, your teammate reads in theirs, and everyone types naturally. You can also flip it off any time with Auto-translate (off).
ch13-xlate.pull: Before: a message you can't read. After: the same message, in your language, in a blink.

diagram.label: FIG. 13.0 — TRANSLATE
diagram.cap: their language → Auto-translate → yours

ch14-open.title: Captions & transcript
ch14-open.standfirst: Canvas M can listen to the room and write it down. A live caption strip floats subtitles at the bottom of a shared screen; a draggable Live transcript panel keeps the full, scrollable history. Both can translate into the language you prefer, line by line. This chapter covers every toggle, state and error you will meet as a participant, and gently points out where the host holds the controls.

ch14-concept.heading: Two views of one stream
ch14-concept.lead: Speech-to-text (STT) turns spoken audio into text in real time. Canvas M shows that text in two places, and both read the same underlying stream — turning a knob in one is reflected in the other.
ch14-concept.body: The Live transcript panel is the full record: every finalised line, oldest at the top, with a speaker name, a timestamp and (optionally) a translation beneath. It is a scrollable history you can drag, resize and leave open. The caption strip is a glance-only layer: a slim glass band pinned to the bottom of whatever is being shared, showing only the newest one to three lines of whoever is speaking right now, then auto-hiding after a few seconds of silence.
ch14-concept.pull: The panel is the record. The strip is the glance. Same words, two windows.

diagram.label: STT feeds both the transcript panel and the caption strip
diagram.cap: One recognition stream, two surfaces: the scrollable panel keeps everything; the strip shows only the freshest lines and collapses to a small CC puck when no one is talking.

note.html: Two kinds of line exist. An interim line is a still-changing guess — it appears dimmed and italic, and is never translated (it would flicker word by word). A final line is locked in; only finals get a translation.

ch14-states.heading: Captions, on and off

tiles.cap: The canvas is clear. Turn them on with Captions (CC) in the header.
A live strip shows the latest spoken lines as people talk.
Open Live transcript for the full record, with per-line translate.

ch14-states.useWhen: Captions help in a noisy room or a second language; open the transcript when you want to scroll back over what was said.

ch15-open.title: Your dashboard
ch15-open.standfirst: Every time you sign in to Canvas M and you are not inside a meeting, the dashboard takes over the whole screen. It is the home base where your meetings, your projects and your calendar all live side by side. This chapter walks every button, panel and badge you will meet there.

ch15-tour.heading: Find your way around the lobby
steps: Press New meeting to start one, or paste a link or code into Join.
Open My projects to browse meetings grouped by project.
Check the Calendar for what's upcoming, today, and tomorrow.
Open the notification bell for invitations awaiting your reply.
Guests land on the portal — your meetings with MAP, ready to Join or Review.
ch15-tour.outcome: You can reach any meeting you're part of from one place.

note.html: A meeting starting soon raises a due notice — press Join now, or Later to dismiss it.

ch15-notif.heading: Notifications, at a glance
rows: You've been invited to a meeting.
Accept or Decline; accepting a live one joins it.
A meeting you're in starts now.
Join now, or Later to dismiss.
Accept to join on the spot.
A log of what you've done.

note.html: The bell is your to-do list; My activity is the history of what already happened.

ch16-open.title: Settings & profile
ch16-open.standfirst: One window holds everything you can change about your own account and this device: your display name and avatar, your read-only organisation details, your password, every meeting preference, the data we keep, and your microphone consent. Open it from the meeting header gear or the dashboard account menu, and every control here behaves exactly like its inline twin.

legend.text: Profile — name, company, avatar
Account & Security — email, password
Preferences — language, theme, translation, STT, captions
My data — what's stored about you

ch16-profile.heading: Set your name, company, and avatar
steps: Open Account settings and select the Profile tab (you usually land here).
Type into Display name — placeholder e.g. Luan Le, up to 48 characters. The live preview and the Save button enable as soon as it is non-blank.
Optionally fill Company — placeholder e.g. MAP Architects, also up to 48 characters.
Pick a built-in tile from the Avatar gallery, or press ⬆ Upload image to choose your own picture.
Press Save. The window stays open; there is no Cancel button here — the header Close is the dismiss.
ch16-profile.outcome: Your new name, company, and avatar save to this device and broadcast to everyone in the meeting — your participant tile, cursor label, and the built-in avatar list all update at once. A library avatar (a lib: pick) also syncs to your account, so it follows your login to other browsers; an uploaded image stays on this device only.
ch16-profile.note: Display name is required: with the field blank the preview shows the placeholder and Save stays disabled. Leading and trailing spaces are trimmed before saving.

host.html: Nothing here renames or removes other people — this tab only ever edits your own identity. Host controls for moderating participants live in the meeting, not in Settings.

ch16-profile.figcap: The Profile tab — name, company, avatar gallery, and the live preview.

ch17-open.title: Leaving & review
ch17-open.standfirst: Every meeting has a way out, and most have an afterlife. This chapter covers the difference between hanging up your call, walking out of the room, and the moment a host ends the meeting for everyone — and what a finished meeting lets you do when you open it again to read the record.

ch17-leave.heading: Leaving the meeting
steps: Find the Leave button at the far-right edge of the header (the arrow-out-of-box icon).
Click it. There's no confirmation prompt — leaving is a safe, reversible action.
Your canvas is saved automatically before the connection closes.
The room is removed from the address bar, so a reload won't pull you back in.
You return to your project home, where the meeting may still be offered as Resume meeting if it's still running.
ch17-leave.outcome: You're out of the room. The meeting carries on for everyone who stayed, and you can re-open it any time it's still live.
ch17-leave.note: If the host removes you from the meeting, you'll see a notice and then be taken out the same way — you don't have to click Leave yourself.
ch17-leave.figcap: The Leave button sits in the header's exit group, away from the live media controls so it's never hit by accident.

ch18-open.title: When something goes wrong
ch18-open.standfirst: A mic that won't unmute, a camera that won't start, a waiting room that won't let you in. Most snags in Canvas M show their own fix right on the button. This chapter reads the exact words the app shows you, names the cause, and gives you the one move that clears it.

ch18-mic.heading: Microphone won't work

rows.sym: Mic icon is red and tooltip reads “This device has no microphone — listen only”
rows.cause: No microphone exists on this device, so you joined in listen-only mode. You can hear everyone but can't speak.
rows.fix: Plug in or enable a microphone, then leave and rejoin the call. On a phone, check that a headset is connected.

rows.sym: Tooltip reads “Microphone denied — enable it in browser settings and retry.”
rows.cause: You blocked the mic permission, so the browser refused access (a NotAllowedError).
rows.fix: Open your browser's site settings, allow the microphone for this site, then click the red mic button to Retry.

rows.sym: Tooltip reads “Microphone is in use by another app (Teams / Zoom). Quit it and retry.”
rows.cause: Another program has grabbed the mic exclusively (a NotReadableError).
rows.fix: Close Teams, Zoom, or any other call app, then click the mic button to Retry.

rows.sym: Tooltip reads “Requesting mic permission…” and the button shows a spinner
rows.cause: The browser's permission prompt is open. Canvas M only asks for the mic the first time you unmute or turn on speech-to-text — not when you join.
rows.fix: Answer the browser prompt with Allow. The spinner clears as soon as you respond.

rows.sym: Tooltip reads “Could not start microphone” with a click-to-retry hint
rows.cause: A generic mic error the browser didn't classify. The raw detail rides the native tooltip.
rows.fix: Click the red mic button to Retry. If it persists, reload the page and rejoin.

rows.sym: Live transcript shows “No local mic stream — this device is in listen-only mode.”
rows.cause: You turned on speech-to-text but have no working mic, so there is nothing to transcribe.
rows.fix: Give the mic permission (or attach a mic) and unmute. Speech-to-text follows your live mic once it's flowing.

ch18-mic.note: Joining is deliberately mic-free: clicking Join enters listening-only and the browser asks for the mic only on your first unmute. That later click is itself the gesture the browser needs to show its prompt.

rows.sym: Camera won't start
rows.cause: Permission or no device
rows.fix: Allow the camera in browser settings, then Turn on camera again.

rows.sym: No blur option
rows.cause: On a phone or tablet
rows.fix: Background effects are desktop-only — present from a computer.

rows.sym: Can't share screen
rows.cause: Someone else is presenting, or iPad/iPhone
rows.fix: Wait for them to finish, or share from a computer.

rows.sym: File won't upload
rows.cause: Unsupported type
rows.fix: Only image, PDF, DXF, and IFC are accepted.

rows.sym: Can't delete a file
rows.cause: It's locked by someone
rows.fix: Ask the locker — or the uploader — to unlock it first.

note.html: Same as the page before — symptom → cause → fix, with a page to turn to.

ch19-open.title: Projects
ch19-open.standfirst: A project is the folder every meeting lives in. It carries the client, the code, the phase and — most importantly — the people who may organise inside it. This chapter covers the dedicated Manage projects page: creating a project with full metadata, editing it, building the member roster, delegating authority, dressing it with a colour and icon, and deleting it when its work is done. Everything here is a host or manager action.

ch19-concept.heading: One project, many meetings
ch19-concept.lead: Every meeting belongs to a project — a named workstream like 20260617 or Africa, each at a phase (Concept, Schematic Design). The project holds its meetings, its files, and its guest list, so nothing scatters.
ch19-concept.body: Open Manage projects from the sidebar to see them all. Pick a project before you create a meeting or invite a client, and everything you do is filed under it.
ch19-concept.pull: Start with the project. Meetings, files and guests all hang off it.

diagram.label: STRUCTURE
diagram.cap: project → meetings · files · guests

ch19-create.heading: Create a project with full metadata
steps: Click New project — at the top of the Manage projects page, in the empty state, or in the sidebar footer. All three open the same modal, titled Create new project.
Fill in the Name (required) and optionally a cover image, project code, client, location, branch/office, phase, project type and description.
Click Save. The app first creates the project by name, then saves the extra fields in a second step.
On success the modal closes and you land in the new project's detail — ready to add members, the natural next step.
If the create call itself fails, the modal stays open with everything you typed so you can retry; the toast reads “Couldn't create the project — check your network and try again.”
ch19-create.outcome: The new project is created with you as its leader and owner. There is only one create path — full metadata in one modal — so no half-configured folders.
ch19-create.note: If the name saves but the extra details don't, you still land in the project, with the toast “Project created, but saving extra details failed — press Edit to retry.” Nothing you typed for the name is lost; re-enter the rest via Edit project.

host.html: Any internal (non-guest) account may create a project. Creating one grants no cross-project power — it simply opens your own folder.

ch20-open.title: Scheduling a meeting
ch20-open.standfirst: One form does two jobs. It can spin up a room and drop you straight into it, or it can plant a meeting on a future date, stamp it with an agenda, name a host, and quietly invite everyone who needs to be there. This chapter walks the whole form, field by field, exactly as the app draws it.

ch20-create.heading: Create & join a meeting
steps: Press + New meeting. Confirm the project at the top.
Give it a title, and an agenda — a topic and notes.
Set Type, Discipline, Priority, and Confidentiality.
Assign a Host (you by default) and an optional Co-host.
Press Create & join.
ch20-create.outcome: You're hosting, on a fresh canvas.

note.html: Leave the title blank and it borrows the agenda topic — but a clear title helps everyone find it later.

ch20-fields.heading: What each field means
rows: Filters and colours it on the calendar
Sorts and flags it on the dashboard
The host admits guests and ends the meeting

note.html: Waiting room for guests is on the way — when live, guests knock and you admit them.

ch21-open.title: Inviting clients
ch21-open.standfirst: Clients and outside guests don't get an account — they get a guest ID: a synthetic login and a one-time password you issue, scoped to a single project. Each guest is also a small contact card — representative, email, company, phone, address, country, and a logo — that you keep alongside the credentials. This chapter covers issuing, copying, editing, resetting, and retiring guests, both from inside a project and from the all-projects Guest manager.

ch21-concept.heading: Staff sign in; guests get a link
ch21-concept.lead: Your colleagues already have accounts. A guest — a client or partner — does not, so you issue them a one-time login link tied to one project. They see only what that project shares.
ch21-concept.body: Guests are managed per project from Guest manager. Each gets an address like name.xxxx@client.canvas.app and a backdrop picked from their country. Retire a guest and their link stops working.
ch21-concept.pull: A guest sees one project — never your whole workspace.

diagram.label: ACCESS
diagram.cap: staff = account · guest = per-project link

ch21-issue.heading: Issue a guest ID
steps: Open the issue form — expand Project guests on a project's detail page (or use Add guest), or open Guest manager from the dashboard nav.
In the Guest manager only: open the Project picker and choose the project to issue into. It defaults to your first manageable project.
Type the client's Representative name (placeholder e.g. Nam). This is the only required field.
Optionally fill Email (optional), Company, Phone, and Address — reference details for your records.
Optionally pick a Country from the flag list to set the client's entry-page backdrop; leave it on Country (picks backdrop) for the default.
Press Issue guest ID. The button reads Issuing… while it works.
ch21-issue.outcome: A new guest ID is minted for the chosen project and the credentials panel appears below the form, headed Guest ID issued. The form clears, and the guest now appears in the list grouped under its project.
ch21-issue.note: Issue guest ID stays disabled until both a project is selected and Representative has real (non-space) text — leading and trailing spaces are trimmed before the name is saved. If the server rejects the request you get a toast: Couldn't issue the guest ID.

host.html: There is no self-service join link for clients here — guests don't request access, you issue it. If a client says they can't get in, check that you've sent them the synthetic Login from the credentials panel, not their email address.

ch21-issue.figcap: The issue form: project picker, the Guest details grid, and Issue guest ID.

ch22-open.title: Hosting the meeting
ch22-open.standfirst: From the moment you press Start meeting to the moment you press End meeting, you hold the room. This chapter walks the host's powers in order — starting a scheduled meeting, inviting the right people, letting guests in from the waiting room, moderating who speaks and who stays, and ending cleanly so an AI recap is waiting for everyone afterwards. Every label here is the one you will see on screen.

ch22-controls.heading: Run the room
steps: Admit guests who knock from the waiting room, when enabled.
Promote a trusted colleague to Co-host to share the load.
Watch the participant count and the live timer in the header.
Use Leave to step out — or end the meeting for everyone when done.
ch22-controls.outcome: The meeting runs on your call.

host.html: These controls appear only for the host and co-host — regular participants never see them.

legend.text: The Canvas M wordmark. On first arrival it plays a brief cinematic reveal centre-screen, then dissolves to hand off to the card. If your device is set to reduce motion, the intro is skipped and the card appears at once.
The language and theme switcher (VI / EN / KO and a light/dark toggle), tucked into the top bar of the form pane.
The strapline “Architectural collaboration platform”, the Login heading, and the subtitle “Sign in to your account”.
The sign-in form. By default this is the email and password form; two link buttons below it switch to the other two ways in.

The brand panel on the right — “Design reviews, in real time” — listing what waits inside: realtime collaboration, BIM & CAD viewers, AI meeting intelligence, and multilingual support. It is decorative; there is nothing to click here.
At the foot of the form: “Need help? Contact your administrator.”

ch1-password.heading: Sign in with email and password
steps: In the Email field, type your work address — the placeholder shows the expected shape, you@company.com.
In the Password field, type your password. The characters stay hidden.
Click Sign In. While it works, the button reads Signing in… and is disabled so you can't submit twice.
On success the card simply disappears and your project home opens.
ch1-password.outcome: You land signed in, ready to open or join a project.
ch1-password.note: The Sign In button stays greyed out until both the email and password fields have something in them. If the email isn't a plausible address (no @ or no domain), you'll see “That email looks invalid.” before any sign-in is even attempted.
ch1-password.figcap: The email and password form is what the card shows by default.

ch1-modes.heading: Pick the form that fits you

tiles.cap: The default. Email + Password, then Sign In. Two links sit underneath to switch to the other two modes.
For guests with no password. Enter just your Email, click Send login link, and Canvas M emails you a one-time link to click.
For when someone sent you an invite. Paste the link or ID,KEY, click Continue, then sign in — you'll be carried straight into that meeting.

ch1-modes.useWhen: Staff use Password; outside guests use the Login link; anyone holding an invite can start from Meeting link. You can switch between them freely — the links below each form toggle modes and clear any error as they do.

ch1-guest.heading: Get a one-time login link by email
steps: On the password form, click Guest? Get a login link by email.
Type your Email. (No password field appears — this way in doesn't use one.)
Click Send login link; while it sends, the button reads Signing in….
Read the confirmation: “Login link sent to [your email]. Open the email to join.”
Switch to your inbox and click the link in the email Canvas M just sent.
To go back without sending, click ← Sign in with a password.
ch1-guest.outcome: Clicking the emailed link returns you to Canvas M already signed in — no password required.
ch1-guest.note: The link is one-time and tied to that email address. If it doesn't arrive within a minute, check spam, then send it again. If you originally arrived from a meeting invite, the link still carries you into that meeting once you return.
ch1-guest.figcap: The guest form asks only for an email.

ch1-link.heading: Start from a meeting link
steps: On the password form, click Have a meeting link?.
Paste your invite into the Meeting link field — a full link, a #room=… fragment, or a bare ID,KEY all work; the placeholder reads “Paste meeting link or ID,KEY”.
Click Continue. The button is disabled until the field has text.
Canvas M saves the meeting and confirms: “Meeting link saved — sign in to join.”, then returns you to the password form.
Sign in with your password (or switch to the guest link). Once you're in, Canvas M joins the saved meeting automatically.
ch1-link.outcome: You are dropped straight into the meeting the invite pointed at, no extra navigation.
ch1-link.note: Pasting a meeting link does not skip signing in — it only remembers where you're headed. Everyone signs in first. If what you paste isn't a recognisable link, you'll see “That meeting link looks invalid.”
ch1-link.figcap: The meeting-link form accepts a link, a fragment, or a bare ID,KEY.

ch1-langtheme.heading: Set the language and theme
ch1-langtheme.lead: The login card carries the same compact control you'll see throughout the app, sitting in the top bar of the form pane — so you can pick the language and the light or dark look before you've even signed in.
ch1-langtheme.body:
Language. Three segments — VI, EN, and KO — switch the whole interface between Vietnamese, English, and Korean. The active one is highlighted. The choice applies immediately and is remembered on this device for next time.

Theme. The sun / moon button toggles between light and dark; its tooltip reads “Toggle light / dark”. A sun icon means you're in light mode, a moon means dark. Like the language, your choice sticks on this device.
ch1-langtheme.pull: Set your language and theme on the way in — the choices travel with you into the app.

note.html: Language and theme are stored on the device you're using, not on your account. Switch computers and you may need to set them again.

ch1-errors.heading: Sign-in messages and what they mean

rows.sym: “Wrong email or password.”
rows.cause: The email and password didn't match an account.
rows.fix: Re-check both, mind capital letters in the password, and try again. If it persists, contact your administrator.

rows.sym: “That email looks invalid.”
rows.cause: What you typed isn't a valid email shape (missing <kbd>@</kbd> or domain). Shown before any sign-in attempt.
rows.fix: Correct the address — it should look like <kbd>you@company.com</kbd>.

rows.sym: “Can't reach the sign-in server. Check your internet connection (or try mobile data).”
rows.cause: Your device couldn't reach the authentication server — often a Wi-Fi or network block, not a wrong password.
rows.fix: Check your connection. A telling sign: it fails on office Wi-Fi but works on mobile data.

rows.sym: “Too many attempts. Please wait a minute and try again.”
rows.cause: Sign-in was rate-limited after several rapid tries.
rows.fix: Wait about a minute, then try once more.

rows.sym: “That meeting link looks invalid.”
rows.cause: The text pasted into the meeting-link field couldn't be read as a link or <kbd>ID,KEY</kbd>.
rows.fix: Re-copy the whole invite from the source and paste it again.

ch1-errors.note: Notice the difference between a credential problem and a network one. “Wrong email or password” means try different details; the connection message means your details are probably fine but your device can't reach the server — don't keep retyping a good password.

ch2-paths.heading: One button, three doors
ch2-paths.lead: Joining is always login-first. There is no anonymous room URL to paste — access is by explicit invitation, and the server checks who you are before it hands back the room key. So the journey always starts the same way: sign in, find the meeting, press Join. What happens next depends on the meeting's state, not on anything you click.
ch2-paths.body: Press Join on a meeting and Canvas M sends you down exactly one of three paths. If the meeting is live and you are internal staff, you go straight onto the canvas. If it is scheduled and has not started, you land on a “Meeting hasn't started yet” waiting screen until the host presses Start. If you are an external guest, you may land in a waiting room and knock to be let in. You never choose the door — the app picks it from the meeting's status and your role.
ch2-paths.pull: There is no room link to share. You join meetings you were invited to — nothing else opens.

diagram.label: The join router
diagram.cap: Press Join, then the meeting's status decides: live → straight in; scheduled → start gate; guest into a live room → waiting room.

note.html: Joining a call never asks for your microphone up front. You enter listening-only, and the browser's mic permission prompt fires later — the first time you unmute or turn on captions.

ch2-find.heading: From the home screen to the room
steps: Sign in. Internal staff land on the project home; external guests land on a single-column list titled “Your meetings with MAP”.
Locate the meeting. Guests see two sections — “Happening now / Upcoming” and “Finished”; staff open a project to see its meetings.
Press Join on a live or upcoming meeting. (A finished meeting shows Review instead — read-only.)
Wait a moment while Canvas M resolves the room and connects — the canvas takes over the screen.
If you left a meeting open earlier, use the Resume meeting banner near the top of the home screen to drop straight back in.
ch2-find.outcome: The lobby disappears and the live meeting canvas fills the screen. You are in the meeting — but not yet in the audio/video call (that is a separate, deliberate step covered later).
ch2-find.note: If your meeting isn't listed, you haven't been invited yet. Guests see the empty-state line “No meetings yet — MAP will add you here.” Ask the organizer to add you; there is no link you can paste to get in.

host.html: Starting, scheduling and inviting people are organizer/host actions reached from the project view and the in-meeting Invite button. As a participant you only ever Join.

ch2-find.figcap: The guest portal lists only the meetings you were invited to, split into upcoming and finished.

ch2-gate.heading: When the meeting hasn't started

tiles.cap: A scheduled meeting you've opened early. You see “Meeting hasn't started yet”, the scheduled time, and a spinner reading “Waiting for the host to start the meeting…” The app polls every few seconds and drops you straight in the instant the host starts.
A terminal notice: “Meeting cancelled” with “The organizer cancelled this meeting.” There is no way forward — use Back to home.
Shown to guests if the meeting finished before they got in: “Meeting has ended” and “This meeting has ended. The organizer will share a recap with you separately.”

ch2-gate.useWhen: You'll see one of these whenever you open a meeting that isn't live yet. The waiting screen is patient — you can leave it open and it will auto-join you when the meeting goes live. Every state offers Back to home to return to your meeting list.

ch2-knock.heading: Knocking to be let in
steps: Press Join on a live meeting as an external guest. Canvas M knocks for you and shows a door-shaped card titled “Waiting to be let in”.
Read the confirmation: the meeting name, “Joining as {your name}”, and a spinner reading “Waiting for the host to let you in…”
Wait. The card checks your status automatically every few seconds — no need to refresh.
When the host admits you, the screen connects you straight into the meeting, muted.
If the host declines, you'll see “Not admitted” with “The host hasn't let you in right now. You can knock again in a moment.”
Press Knock again to retry. There is a short cooldown, so wait a moment if it doesn't take immediately.
ch2-knock.outcome: On admission you arrive in the meeting with your microphone off — nothing is broadcast until you choose to join the call and unmute.
ch2-knock.note: Internal staff never see the waiting room — they're admitted automatically. The waiting room is only for external guests entering a live meeting. Use Back to home at any point to leave the queue.

host.html: Admitting and declining knocks is a host control, shown to the host as a “Waiting to join” section in the participants panel with Admit and Deny buttons.

ch2-knock.figcap: The guest waiting room: your name, the meeting title, and a live spinner while the host decides.

legend.text: Canvas M wordmark — the brand mark; tells you which app you're in.
Meeting title — the project name above the meeting name (or “Untitled meeting”). It's static text for you; only the organizer sees an edit chevron.
Elapsed timer — the clock icon shows time since the host started; tooltip “Meeting time elapsed.” Late joiners see the same shared time, not their own.
People count — the head-count in the room; a small mic badge shows how many are in the audio call. Click it to open the Participants panel.
Media group — join/leave the call, mic, camera, raise-hand, reactions and present sit here (covered next).
Captions & transcript — the Captions (CC) toggle and the Transcript button (with a live segment count).
Leave — the door/arrow icon, tooltip “Leave”: you exit the room; everyone else stays.

ch2-call.heading: Being in the meeting vs. being in the call

tiles.cap: Being on the canvas does not put you in the call. An open-door button (tooltip “Join”) sits in the media group. Press it to enter the call — listening-only, no mic prompt yet. While it connects you see a spinner, tooltip “Requesting mic permission…”

The cluster expands: Mic (Mute/Unmute), Camera (Turn on/off camera, off by default), Raise hand, Reactions (👍 ❤️ 😂 🎉 👏 😮) and Leave call (phone-down). Your first unmute is when the browser asks for the microphone.

A red mic-off button carries the reason in its tooltip and click retries: “Microphone denied…”, “Microphone is in use by another app…”, or “Couldn't join the call — check your network and try again.” No microphone at all shows “Listening” / “This device has no microphone — listen only.”

ch2-call.useWhen: Join the call when you want to hear and speak. Leave call (phone-down) hangs up the audio/video only — you stay on the canvas. That is different from Leave in the header (you exit the meeting). Both are different again from the host's red End meeting.

ch2-refs.heading: The three “exit” verbs, and what each control says
rows: Enters the audio/video call, listening-only — no mic prompt yet.
Toggles your microphone. First unmute triggers the browser permission prompt.
Turn on camera / Turn off camera
Off by default; opt-in. Disabled with a reason if no camera is detected.
Signals the host; peers see your hand raised.
Fires a quick emoji (👍 ❤️ 😂 🎉 👏 😮) to the room.
Hangs up audio/video; you stay on the canvas.
You exit the meeting; everyone else stays in the room.
Drops out of the waiting/start gate and returns to your meeting list.

host.html: A red power icon (“End meeting”) appears only for the host/organizer/co-host and switches everyone to read-only review. As a participant you won't see it.

ch2-trouble.heading: Common snags and how to clear them

rows.sym: My meeting isn't in the list
rows.cause: You haven't been invited, or the invite was revoked
rows.fix: Ask the organizer to add you. Guests see “No meetings yet — MAP will add you here.” — there's no link to paste in.

rows.sym: Stuck on “Waiting for the host to start”
rows.cause: The meeting is scheduled and hasn't been started
rows.fix: Leave it open — it auto-joins the moment the host starts. Or press Back to home and try again later.

rows.sym: “Not admitted” after knocking
rows.cause: The host declined or hasn't responded
rows.fix: Press Knock again; wait a moment if it doesn't take — there's a short cooldown.

rows.sym: “Meeting cancelled” / “Meeting has ended”
rows.cause: The organizer cancelled or ended the meeting
rows.fix: These are terminal. The organizer shares a recap separately. Use Back to home.

rows.sym: Red mic button — “Microphone denied”
rows.cause: Browser blocked mic access
rows.fix: Enable the mic in browser settings, then click the button to retry.

rows.sym: “Microphone is in use by another app”
rows.cause: Teams / Zoom (or similar) holds the mic
rows.fix: Quit the other app, then click the red button to retry.

rows.sym: “Couldn't join the call”
rows.cause: Network hiccup reaching the call server
rows.fix: Check your connection and click the red button to retry.

rows.sym: “Listening” — mic is greyed out
rows.cause: No microphone on this device
rows.fix: Expected — you can still hear everyone. Join from a device with a mic to speak.

rows.sym: The host removed me
rows.cause: A host removed you from the meeting
rows.fix: You'll see “The host removed you from the meeting.” Re-join only if you're still invited.

ch2-trouble.note: Every call error button does double duty: the tooltip explains the problem and a single click retries. You rarely need to reload.

ch3-join.heading: Join the call (listener-first)
steps: Open the meeting. The media controls live in the meeting header, not on the canvas, so the drawing surface stays clear.
Find the open-door icon labelled Join. This is the only call button visible before you connect.
Click Join. No microphone prompt appears — you join listening-only.
The button becomes a spinner with the tooltip “Requesting mic permission…” while it connects.
Once connected, the spinner is replaced by the full live cluster: mic, camera, raise-hand, reactions, recording, and a red Leave call button.
ch3-join.outcome: You are now in the audio/video call as a listener. Your microphone has not been touched yet, and your camera is off. Nothing you do is broadcast until you flip a control on.
ch3-join.note: Joining the call is separate from joining the meeting. You can sit on the canvas without ever clicking Join — you simply won't hear or be heard until you do.
ch3-join.figcap: The header media cluster the moment the call goes live.

ch3-mental.heading: Three exits, one entrance
ch3-mental.lead: The single most common confusion in any meeting tool is which button leaves what. Canvas M deliberately gives every exit a distinct glyph so they never collide.
ch3-mental.body: The red phone-down Leave call button (in the media cluster) hangs up only the audio/video call — you stay in the meeting and on the canvas, and can re-Join at any time. Walking out of the meeting entirely is a separate door icon (Leave) further along the header. Ending the meeting for everyone is a third, host-only control (End meeting). Three actions, three icons, no overlap. The open door you click to enter is intentionally not a microphone icon, because entering no longer promises that your mic turns on.

note.html: End meeting closes the room for all participants and switches everyone to read-only review. As a participant you will never see it — only the host does.

ch3-micstates.heading: Reading the microphone button

tiles.cap: No mic on this device. Button disabled, struck-through mic, tooltip “This device has no microphone — listen only”. You hear everyone.
Solid mic icon, tooltip “Mute”. You're transmitting; your tile shows a green live dot.
Struck-through mic painted red, tooltip “Unmute”. Your tile shows a red mic-off badge.

ch3-micstates.useWhen: Glance here whenever you're unsure whether you're being heard — the icon shape, its colour, and the tooltip together tell you the exact state.

ch3-camera.heading: Turn on your camera
steps: Find the camera icon next to the mic. It starts off — a struck-through camera with the tooltip “Turn on camera”.
Click it. While the camera spins up, the icon becomes a brief spinner.
Once live, the icon becomes a solid camera (highlighted as active) and the tooltip reads “Turn off camera”. Your avatar tile is replaced by your live video, mirrored for a natural self-view.
Click again to turn the camera off and return to your avatar.
ch3-camera.outcome: Your camera is opt-in and defaults to off. If your video fails to attach, your tile falls back to your avatar rather than showing a black box.
ch3-camera.note: If this device has no camera, the button is disabled with the tooltip “No camera detected on this device”. If the camera can't start (permissions or busy), the tooltip reads “Couldn't start the camera — check permissions and retry.” and you stay on your avatar.

host.html: Virtual / blurred backgrounds aren't on the call bar — they live in Settings → Preferences. Your saved choice auto-applies whenever your camera turns on.

ch3-handreact.heading: Raise your hand & react
steps: To raise your hand, click the hand icon — tooltip “Raise hand”. It highlights, and a ✋ badge appears on your avatar for everyone to see.
Click it again (now “Lower hand”) to put it down. Leaving the call lowers it automatically.
To react, click the smiley icon — tooltip “Reactions” — to open the emoji popover.
Pick from 👍 ❤️ 😂 🎉 👏 😮. The emoji floats up over your avatar for everyone and fades after a few seconds.
Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> or click outside to close the popover without sending anything.
ch3-handreact.outcome: Your raised hand is sticky and visible to all peers; a reaction is a brief, animated burst. Both broadcast in real time without you having to unmute.
ch3-handreact.note: Raise-hand and reactions are participant gestures — there is no separate host approval. Reactions never make sound; they're purely visual.

legend.text: People strip — every participant as an avatar (or live video) tile. The chip on the left shows joined / invited and how many are in call.
Your own tile (“You”) is highlighted. Click it to open Your profile (name, company, avatar).
Mic dot / badge — green dot = live, red struck-mic = muted, dimmed tile = not in the call yet.
Crown marks the host; a quieter half-crown marks a Co-host. A 📺 badge means that person is sharing their screen.
✋ raised-hand and floating reaction emojis appear over the relevant avatar.
Click any other person's tile to follow their view (your viewport tracks theirs); press Esc to stop.

ch3-controls-ref.heading: Every live-call control
rows: Connect to the call as a listener — no mic prompt.
Mute · Unmute · This device has no microphone — listen only
Toggle your audio. First unmute triggers the mic permission prompt.
Turn on camera · Turn off camera
Toggle your video. Off by default; falls back to your avatar.
Sticky ✋ on your avatar, visible to all. Cleared on leave.
Send 👍 ❤️ 😂 🎉 👏 😮 — floats over your avatar, fades quickly.
Host-only start/stop. You see a live timer pill naming the host.
Hang up audio/video only — you stay in the meeting.
Switch surface: Minimal, Filmstrip, Gallery, plus Floating presenter.
ch3-controls-ref.note: Tooltips are the exact strings the app shows on hover. When you're reviewing a finished meeting (read-only), the entire mic/join/leave cluster is hidden — there is no live call to join.

host.html: The red record dot is active only for the host. As a participant it appears disabled with a tooltip naming who can record: “Only the host ({host}) can record”. While recording is live you see a status pill: “{host} is recording the meeting · {time}”.

ch3-trouble.heading: Microphone & camera fixes

rows.sym: Mic button is greyed out, tooltip says “listen only”
rows.cause: No microphone on this device, so you joined listener-only.
rows.fix: You can still hear everyone. Plug in a mic / headset and rejoin to speak.

rows.sym: Error icon on the call bar after Join
rows.cause: Mic permission denied.
rows.fix: Tooltip reads “Microphone denied — enable it in browser settings and retry.” Allow the mic in your browser, then click the icon to retry.

rows.sym: Can't unmute — error tooltip mentions another app
rows.cause: Your mic is held by Teams / Zoom or similar.
rows.fix: “Microphone is in use by another app (Teams / Zoom). Quit it and retry.” Close the other app and click to retry.

rows.sym: Camera button disabled
rows.cause: No camera detected on this device.
rows.fix: Tooltip: “No camera detected on this device.” Connect a webcam, then rejoin.

rows.sym: Camera won't turn on
rows.cause: Permission blocked or device busy.
rows.fix: “Couldn't start the camera — check permissions and retry.” Grant camera access in the browser and click again; your avatar shows meanwhile.

rows.sym: Whole call bar is missing
rows.cause: You're reviewing a finished meeting (read-only).
rows.fix: There's no live call here. Open the live meeting link to join a call.

rows.sym: Couldn't join — network message
rows.cause: The call failed to connect.
rows.fix: “Couldn't join the call — check your network and try again.” Click the error icon to retry.

ch3-trouble.note: After any failed join the call button becomes a single red error icon — clicking it retries. The plain-English headline rides the hover tooltip; the raw technical detail is on the native title for support.

ch4-concept.heading: One canvas, three surfaces
ch4-concept.lead: Your meeting always has a video surface — the way camera tiles are arranged around the drawing canvas. Canvas M ships three: Minimal, Filmstrip, and Gallery. They are mutually exclusive: you are always in exactly one.
ch4-concept.body: The choice is yours alone. It is a per-user preference, not synced to the room, so switching layouts changes only your screen — never anyone else's. The same tiles power every surface: each person shows their live camera when it is on, or their avatar when it is off, with a name label and a muted badge. Switching surfaces never rebuilds presence; it only re-arranges the same faces.
ch4-concept.pull: Your layout is yours. Switching never touches anyone else's screen.

diagram.label: Minimal · Filmstrip · Gallery share one set of tiles
diagram.cap: The same per-person tile renders in all three surfaces — the layout only changes where they sit.

note.html: Your chosen layout is remembered across reloads (saved locally on this device). A new device or browser starts back at Minimal.

ch4-switch.heading: Switch your video layout
steps: Find the Video layout button in the meeting header — the small icon whose glyph changes to match your current surface.
Click it to open the popover menu.
Pick a surface: Minimal, Filmstrip, or Gallery. A check mark sits beside the one in use.
The menu closes and your canvas re-arranges instantly.
ch4-switch.outcome: Your video surface changes for you only. The header button's icon updates to reflect the new mode.
ch4-switch.note: Below the three surfaces sits a separator and a fourth row — Floating presenter — covered later in this chapter. It is an overlay, not a surface, so it has its own check mark you can turn on or off independently.
ch4-switch.figcap: The Video layout popover: three radio surfaces plus the Floating presenter toggle.

ch4-modes.heading: Minimal, Filmstrip, Gallery

tiles.cap: Just the avatar strip along the bottom. The canvas stays as large as possible — the default, and the choice when drawing is the point.
A full-width rail of camera tiles docked to the bottom (~140px tall). The canvas is pushed up, not covered, so it stays clean and usable above the faces.
A full-screen grid of everyone's camera, like Zoom or Meet. Opens over the canvas as a dialog; close it to return.

ch4-modes.useWhen: Reach for Minimal while you sketch, Filmstrip when you want faces visible without leaving the canvas, and Gallery for a faces-first moment — a round of intros, a vote, a discussion where the drawing waits.

legend.text: Title bar — reads Meeting followed by a count of how many people are shown (e.g. Meeting · 6).
Grid / Speaker sub-mode toggle. Grid tiles everyone equally; Speaker promotes one face to a big stage with the rest in a rail below.
Close button (✕ Close), top-right — exits the gallery and drops you back to the Minimal strip.
A camera tile — live video, or the avatar when the camera is off. A green ring marks whoever is speaking.
Tile label — the person's name, a (You) tag on your own tile, a Host badge for the host, and a 🔇 icon when they are muted.
Pin affordance — a quiet pin glyph on the auto-focused tile, or an Unpin chip on a tile you pinned yourself.

ch4-focus.heading: Focus and pinning
ch4-focus.lead: Across Filmstrip, the Gallery speaker stage, and the floating window, Canvas M always highlights one focused person — the presenter of the moment. You never have to set this; it resolves automatically, and you can override it with a pin.
ch4-focus.body: The focus follows a strict order of precedence, highest wins: your pin → the person sharing their screen → the active speaker → the host → the first tile. So if nobody is pinned or sharing, the focus simply follows whoever is talking. To pin, click any tile (in the gallery or filmstrip) — it is promoted to focus and shows an Unpin chip. Click it again, or pin someone else, to release it. Pins are local and ephemeral: they affect only your view and clear on reload. If the person you pinned leaves the room, the focus quietly falls back down the chain.
ch4-focus.pull: Pin = your pick. Screen-share, then speaker, then host fill in when you haven't pinned anyone.

diagram.label: Pin › screen-share › active speaker › host › first
diagram.cap: Focus precedence — the highest rule that matches a present person wins.

note.html: Pinning is per-viewer — there is no way to force a focus for the whole room from here. Each person chooses their own pin. Host moderation (mute, remove, admit) lives in the Participants panel, not in the video layout controls.

ch4-floating.heading: The floating presenter window
steps: Open the Video layout popover and turn on Floating presenter (the row below the three surfaces).
A small picture-in-picture card appears over the canvas, showing the focused person's camera (or avatar) with their name.
Drag the card by its header to move it — on release it snaps to the nearest corner, and that corner is remembered.
Click Minimise to shrink it to a small circular puck; click the puck to bring the card back.
Click Hide (×) to dismiss it entirely.
ch4-floating.outcome: You keep watching the presenter in a corner while the canvas stays fully usable. The window shows the same focused person every other surface agrees on.
ch4-floating.note: The floating window only ever shows someone else — never your own face — and it is hidden automatically in Gallery mode, where everyone is already full-screen. The minimise tooltip reads Reopen presenter window on the puck.
ch4-floating.figcap: The floating presenter PiP, snapped to a corner with Minimise and Hide controls.

ch4-ref.heading: Every layout control
rows: Opens the surface popover; its icon mirrors your current surface.
Avatar strip only — canvas stays maximal. The default.
Bottom rail of camera tiles that pushes the canvas up (~140px).
PiP of the focused person over the canvas; off by default.
Tiles everyone equally inside the gallery.
One big focused tile, the rest in a rail below.
Pin that person as focus; click again to Unpin.
Exits the gallery back to the Minimal strip.
ch4-ref.note: Surface (Minimal/Filmstrip/Gallery) and the Grid/Speaker sub-mode are both per-user preferences and both survive a reload. Pins and the Floating-presenter toggle are per-session and clear on reload.

host.html: None of these controls are host-gated — every participant has the full set. They change only your own view.

ch4-trouble.heading: Video layout gotchas

rows.sym: A tile shows an avatar, not video
rows.cause: That person's camera is off (or hasn't started). Tiles only show live video while a camera is actually publishing.
rows.fix: Nothing to fix — it's expected. Their face appears the moment they turn the camera on.

rows.sym: My own tile looks mirrored
rows.cause: Self-view is mirrored on purpose — a front camera reads more naturally that way.
rows.fix: This is intended and affects only your local view; others see you un-mirrored.

rows.sym: The face I pinned jumped to someone else
rows.cause: The pinned person left the room, so focus fell back down the chain (screen-share › speaker › host › first).
rows.fix: Click the tile of the person you want and pin them again.

rows.sym: Floating presenter won't appear
rows.cause: It is hidden in Gallery mode by design, and it never shows your own face when you're the only person.
rows.fix: Switch to Minimal or Filmstrip, and make sure another participant is present.

rows.sym: My layout reset to Minimal on a new device
rows.cause: The preference is saved per-device; a different browser or machine has no saved choice.
rows.fix: Re-pick your surface from the Video layout popover — it'll stick on that device.

rows.sym: The green ring keeps moving between tiles
rows.cause: The ring marks the active speaker, which naturally shifts as people talk.
rows.fix: Pin the person you want fixed in focus to stop the ring driving the stage.

ch4-trouble.note: A camera tile never goes black on a stream error — if a video track fails to attach, the tile quietly falls back to the avatar instead.

ch5-focus-model.heading: One focused person, many surfaces
ch5-focus-model.lead: Canvas M always resolves a single focused person — the presenter the room is built around. Every video surface agrees on who that is, so the big tile in Gallery, the ring in the filmstrip and the floating window never disagree.
ch5-focus-model.body: The focus is computed, not stored. Canvas M walks a strict order of precedence and picks the first match that is still in the room: your manual pin first, then whoever is sharing their screen, then the active speaker, then the host, and finally — if nothing else applies — the first tile. Because it is a pure derivation, focus updates the instant someone starts talking, starts sharing, or leaves; there is nothing to clean up.
ch5-focus-model.pull: Pin beats screen-share beats speaker beats host beats first.

diagram.label: Focus precedence
diagram.cap: The single focused person resolves top-down; the first rule that matches a present participant wins.

note.html: Focus is per-viewer. The person you pin, the surface you choose and the view you follow are all yours alone — they are never broadcast, so picking a different face does not change what anyone else sees.

ch5-raise-hand.heading: Ask to speak without interrupting
steps: Join the call so the live controls appear in the meeting header (see Chapter 4).
Click the hand button. Its tooltip reads Raise hand.
The button turns amber and the tooltip flips to Lower hand — you are now raised.
A sticky ✋ badge appears on the top of your avatar tile, visible to everyone in the room.
Click the hand button again to lower it; the badge clears for all participants.
ch5-raise-hand.outcome: Your raised hand is broadcast to the whole room and stays up until you lower it — there is no auto-timeout.
ch5-raise-hand.note: Leaving the call clears your raised hand automatically, so you never leave a hand stuck up after you go.

host.html: There is no participant control to lower someone else's hand. Hosts mute and remove people from the participant panel, but the hand itself is owned by the person who raised it.

ch5-raise-hand.figcap: The hand button in its raised (amber) state with the ✋ badge on the avatar.

ch5-reactions.heading: Send a quick emoji
steps: In the live header controls, click the smiley button — its tooltip reads Reactions.
A small popover opens with six emoji: 👍 ❤️ 😂 🎉 👏 😮.
Click one to send it; the popover closes and the emoji floats up over your avatar for about three seconds.
Everyone in the room sees the same emoji animate over your tile, then it fades on its own.
Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> or click anywhere outside the popover to close it without sending.
ch5-reactions.outcome: Reactions are transient — they animate for roughly three seconds and then expire by themselves. Nothing is logged and nothing stays on screen.
ch5-reactions.note: Each emoji button is labelled "Send {emoji}" on hover. Reactions float from your own avatar's position, so the room can tell at a glance who reacted.
ch5-reactions.figcap: The reactions popover with its six quick-react emoji.

ch5-follow.heading: Lock your viewport to someone else's
steps: In the participant strip along the bottom, hover any tile that is not your own; the tooltip reads Click to follow their view.
Click the tile. Your viewport zooms and pans to match theirs and stays locked as they move around the canvas.
An 👁 eye badge appears on that person's tile to show you are following them; the tooltip now reads Following — click to stop.
Click the same tile again to stop following — or press <kbd>Esc</kbd> anywhere to release the lock instantly.
Following someone else, or having them leave, also ends the follow.
ch5-follow.outcome: While following, your canvas tracks the other person's visible region automatically — useful when someone is walking the room through a drawing.
ch5-follow.note: Clicking your own tile does not follow anything; it opens your profile editor (display name, company, avatar) instead. The tooltip for your tile reads Your profile.

host.html: Following is a personal, local action — you choose to follow, and only your view moves. No one can force you to follow them, and following someone never moves their view.

ch5-follow.figcap: A followed tile showing the 👁 eye badge.

ch5-pin.heading: Lock the focus onto one face
ch5-pin.lead: A pin is your manual override of the focus order. When you pin someone, their face becomes the focused person on every surface — the big Gallery tile, the filmstrip ring and the floating window — regardless of who is speaking or sharing.
ch5-pin.body: To pin, click any tile in the filmstrip or the gallery. The tooltip reads Click to pin as focus. Click the pinned tile again to unpin — the affordance switches to Unpin — and focus falls back down the precedence chain to the screen-sharer, speaker, or host. A pin is ephemeral and local: it is never sent to other people and a reload clears it. If the person you pinned leaves the room, the pin quietly stops applying and focus moves on.

note.html: Pin and follow are different tools. Pin changes whose face is featured in the video surfaces; follow changes where your canvas is looking. You can do both at once, to the same person or to different people.

ch5-surfaces.heading: Three ways to see the room

tiles.cap: Just the bottom participant strip — avatars (or live camera thumbnails), names, mic dots and badges. The canvas stays fully clear. This is the default.
An opaque rail of camera tiles docked across the bottom (~140px tall). The canvas is pushed up, not covered; the focused person gets a ring. Click a tile to pin it.
A full-screen grid of everyone's camera. A Grid / Speaker toggle switches between an even grid and one big focused tile with the rest in a strip. Close with Close.

ch5-surfaces.useWhen: Pick a surface from the Video layout button in the meeting header. The menu lists Minimal, Filmstrip and Gallery as a single choice, with a checkmark on the active one. Your choice is remembered per device across reloads.

ch5-floating.heading: Keep watching while you work
steps: Open the Video layout menu in the header and toggle Floating presenter on (it sits below the surface choices with its own checkmark).
A small picture-in-picture card of the focused person appears over the canvas, showing their live camera or avatar with their name.
Drag the card by its header (the pin grip); on release it snaps to the nearest of the four corners, and that corner is remembered.
Click − (tooltip Minimise) to shrink it to a small circular puck; click the puck to restore it.
Click × (tooltip Hide) to dismiss the window; reopen it from the same Video layout toggle.
When minimised, the puck's tooltip reads Reopen presenter window.
ch5-floating.outcome: The floating window always shows the same focused person as the other surfaces, and it follows your pin. It is meant for watching someone else while you draw, so it never shows your own face when there is anyone else to watch.
ch5-floating.note: The floating window only appears over the Minimal and Filmstrip surfaces. In Gallery it is hidden automatically, because the gallery already shows everyone full-screen.
ch5-floating.figcap: The floating presenter card docked to a corner, with its minimise and hide buttons.

ch5-states.heading: Tile badges & indicators
rows: In the call with mic on.
In the call but muted; tile tooltip Muted.
In the room but has not joined the audio call yet.
You are following this person's view.
Active speaker — the same ring used across all surfaces.
ch5-states.note: Only your own tile and the current speaker show a name on the strip by default; everyone else shows their name in a hover tooltip. The left-hand count chip reads Joined / Invited and opens the full participant panel when clicked.

host.html: Hover a peer's tile as host to reveal Mute this participant and Remove from meeting buttons; the same actions live in the participant panel under each person. Guests never see these, even if host election briefly lands on them.

ch5-trouble.heading: When presence misbehaves

rows.sym: Following stopped on its own
rows.cause: You pressed Esc, clicked another tile, or the person you followed left the room.
rows.fix: Click their tile again to re-follow once they are back. Esc always releases the lock.

rows.sym: The floating presenter vanished
rows.cause: You switched to the Gallery surface, where the floating window is hidden by design.
rows.fix: Switch back to Minimal or Filmstrip, or use the full-screen gallery instead.

rows.sym: My pin disappeared after reload
rows.cause: Pins are ephemeral and per-viewer — a reload always clears them.
rows.fix: Click the tile to pin again. Use it for in-the-moment focus, not a permanent setting.

rows.sym: The floating window shows the wrong face
rows.cause: With no pin, it tracks the resolved focus (screen-sharer, then speaker, then host).
rows.fix: Click a tile in the filmstrip or gallery to pin the face you want.

rows.sym: I can't lower someone else's raised hand
rows.cause: A raised hand is owned by the person who raised it; there is no override.
rows.fix: Ask them to lower it, or mute them from the host controls if you are the host.

rows.sym: My reaction didn't stay on screen
rows.cause: Reactions are transient and expire after about three seconds.
rows.fix: This is expected — send another if you need to signal again.

ch5-trouble.note: If your own tile looks dimmed with no mic indicator, you are in the room but have not joined the audio call. Join from the header door button (Chapter 4).

ch6-two-backgrounds.heading: Two backgrounds, two homes
ch6-two-backgrounds.lead: The word “background” means two distinct things in Canvas M, and they are set in two different places. Knowing which is which saves a lot of hunting.
ch6-two-backgrounds.body:
Dashboard wallpaper is the image or gradient painted behind the glass panes of your lobby — the home screen where your meetings and projects live. You change it from the small image button in the lobby header (its tooltip reads Hình nền). It affects only what you see on your own desk; nobody else is touched.

Camera background is the blur or scene that replaces the real room behind you in your outgoing camera feed during a meeting. Everyone in the call sees it. You set it from Account settings → Preferences, under Change / blur background. Below it sits Video quality, which controls how crisp that same camera feed is.
ch6-two-backgrounds.pull: Wallpaper is for your eyes only. Camera background and quality are what the room sees.

diagram.label: Where each background lives
diagram.cap: Lobby header (left) owns the dashboard wallpaper; Account settings → Preferences (right) owns the camera background and video quality.

note.html: All three preferences are stored in this browser’s local storage, not on your account. Sign in on another computer and you start from the defaults again. This is by design — they are purely cosmetic.

ch6-wallpaper.heading: Set your lobby wallpaper
steps: On your dashboard, find the small picture icon in the lobby header (next to the notification bell). Its label is Hình nền (“Wallpaper”).
Click it. A small glass popover titled Hình nền opens with a grid of tiles.
Click any tile to apply it instantly — the desk repaints behind the panes as you click. The active tile shows a highlighted border.
To use your own picture, click the last tile, Tải ảnh lên (“Upload image”), and choose an image file. Canvas M resizes and compresses it before saving.
To go back to the plain glass desk, click the Mặc định (“Default”) tile, or click the small × on your uploaded tile.
Click anywhere outside the popover to close it.
ch6-wallpaper.outcome: Your chosen wallpaper paints behind the glass and is remembered on this browser. The image renders sharp — the frosted look comes from the glass panes in front of it, not from blurring the photo.
ch6-wallpaper.note: Labels in this picker are in Vietnamese regardless of your interface language — this small lobby control is not yet translated.
ch6-wallpaper.figcap: The Hình nền popover: five preset tiles plus an upload tile.

ch6-wallpaper-tiles.heading: The wallpaper choices

tiles.cap: Default — the plain Glass-Desk gradient, no image.
Forest mist — a soft photographic preset.
Crystal leaves — a photographic preset.
Olive champagne — a dark low-chroma gradient.
Pastel day — a bright low-chroma gradient.

tiles.state: Tải ảnh lên / Ảnh của bạn
tiles.cap: Upload your own — becomes “Ảnh của bạn” (Your image) once set, with an × to remove.

ch6-wallpaper-tiles.useWhen: Pick a photographic preset for warmth, a gradient for a calm low-distraction desk, or upload a company image. The two gradients are tuned so the glass panes stay readable on top.

ch6-camera-bg.heading: Blur or replace your camera background
steps: Open Your profile from the meeting header (the gear / avatar control), which opens the Account settings modal.
Click the Preferences tab in the left rail.
Scroll to Change / blur background. You’ll see a row of chips and a row of scene thumbnails.
Click No background for the raw camera, or a Blur chip — Light, Medium, or Strong — for progressively heavier blur.
Or click a scene thumbnail — Forest mist, Crystal leaves, or Office — to drop yourself in front of that image.
Only one choice is ever active (it’s a single radio group); the active chip or thumbnail is highlighted.
